ety.text: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آبدست (âbdest), from Classical Persian آبدست (ābdast).

s.g: arboretum (place of many varieties of trees)

x: — Ну, слу́шай, ба́ба. Ма́зями да ка́плями тут не помо́жешь. На́до его́ в больни́це оста́вить.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle Russian больница (bolʹnica), attested in 16-17ᵗʰ c. By surface analysis, боль (bolʹ) + -ница (-nica). Cognate with Old Ruthenian больница (bolʹnica), болница (bolnica), Church Slavonic больни́ца (bolĭníca), whence South Slavic: Bulgarian болница (bolnica), Macedonian болница (bolnica), Serbo-Croatian болница, Slovene bolnišnica, Slovene bolnica. Note Czech nemocnice (i.e. **немочница), Lower Sorbian chórownja (i.e. **хворобня).
Borrowed from French bore or from German Bor.
Borrowed from German bohren (“to bore, to drill”). Doublet of бур (bur).

s.g: Borneo (a large island of Southeast Asia, politically divided between Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia)

x: Ка́ждый гость, приезжа́я к ним, отдава́л свой долг меланхоли́ческому настрое́нию хозя́йки и пото́м занима́лся и све́тскими разгово́рами, и та́нцами, и у́мственными и́грами, и турни́рами буриме́, кото́рые бы́ли в мо́де у Карагиных.

s.g: according to one's understanding; as far as one can understand with the data and knowledge available at the moment
to suck in, to drink in
to celebrate (with a ceremony or a song)

to give out, to pay out, to hand, to issue, to distribute

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic вꙑдавати (vydavati), from Proto-Slavic *vydavati. By surface analysis, вы- (vy-) + дава́ть (davátʹ).

s.g: to graze, to pasture, to drive cattle to pasture

ety.text: Calque of Latin pecūnia nōn olet.

x: Ни про́сьбы, ни увеща́ния гра́фа и поме́щика, вступи́вшегося за моего́ о́тчима, — ничто́ не могло́ поколеба́ть доно́счика в его́ наме́рении.

s.g: a surname, Zhuravlyov and Zhuravlev, equivalent to English Crane

ety.text: Borrowed from German kapitulieren (“to capitulate”), from Latin capitulare, from capitulum, diminutive form of caput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *káput (“head”).
Omitting several steps, from Latin cōnfūsus, from Latin cōnfundō (whence also English confound), from Latin con- + Latin fundō.

s.g: ledoyom (intermontane depressions which might get completely filled by glaciers from the surrounding mountains at the maxima of glaciation, creating esker-like depressions under the ice)

ety.text: From лед- (led-) + -о- (-o-) + -ём (-jóm), combining form of имать (imatʹ, “to take, originally to have”) (compare 1sg. present е́млю (jémlju)). Formed by analogy with водоём (vodojóm).
Old East Slavic лише (liše), originally comparative form of лихъ (lixŭ, “bad”). Compare with Ukrainian лише́ (lyšé), лишень (lyšenʹ) and лиш (lyš), Carpathian Rusyn лиш (lyš).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic митрополиꙗ (mitropolija), from Medieval Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).

s.g: toilet room (especially a poorly cleaned or poorly equipped one)

ety.text: From Пара́ша (Paráša), according to the popular name of the holiday of Saint Paraskeva of the Balkans – Параске́ва Грязни́ха (celebrated on 27 October); the name was given due to the autumn mud and bad weather.

s.g: The folk holiday of Saint Paraskeva of the Balkans, falling on October 17.

ety.text: Derived from Параске́ва Грязни́ха (Paraskéva Grjazníxa), the holiday of Saint Paraskeva of the Balkans.
Influenced by пара́ша (paráša, “a prison toilet, after the rainy conditions from Paraskeva's feast day”) + Ра́ша (Ráša, “Russia”).

s.g: a vile person, bastard, scoundrel, asshole

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *paskǫda. Cognate with Ukrainian па́скуд (páskud), паску́да (paskúda), Belarusian по́скудзь (póskudzʹ), Polish paskuda, Old East Slavic паскудьнъ (paskudĭnŭ, “poor”) (compare modern Russian паску́дный (paskúdnyj, “low, mean”)). By surface analysis, па- (pa-) + ску́д(ный) (skúd(nyj)) + -а (-a).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *paskǫda. Cognate with Ukrainian па́скуд (páskud), паску́да (paskúda), Belarusian по́скудзь (póskudzʹ), Polish paskuda, Old East Slavic паскудьнъ (paskudĭnŭ, “poor”) (compare modern Russian паску́дный (paskúdnyj, “low, mean”)). By surface analysis, па- (pa-) + ску́д(ный) (skúd(nyj)) + -а (-a).

x: Весьма́ вероя́тно и то, что Катери́не Ива́новне захоте́лось, и́менно при э́том слу́чае, и́менно в ту мину́ту, когда́ она́, каза́лось бы, все́ми на све́те оста́влена, показа́ть всем э́тим «ничто́жным и скве́рным жильца́м», что она́ не то́лько «уме́ет жить и уме́ет приня́ть», но что совсе́м да́же не…

ety.text: From Old Church Slavonic рьдьръ (rĭdĭrŭ) (Russian), via vowel assimilation from *ръдьръ (*rŭdĭrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rъdrъ; cognate with Old East Slavic ръдръ (rŭdrŭ). рьдьръ (rĭdĭrŭ) + -ый (-yj) developed to *ре́дрый (*rédryj), then to the modern form рёдрый (rjódryj) by diphthongization (see History of the Russian language § The yo vowel on Wikipedia).

s.g: Severnaya Zemlya (an archipelago of Krasnoyarsk Krai, in the north of Russia in the Arctic Ocean)

initialism of Социалисти́ческая Федерати́вная Респу́блика Югосла́вия (Socialistíčeskaja Federatívnaja Respúblika Jugoslávija) (= Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia), official name of Yugoslavia: a former Communist country in Southeastern Europe that existed from 1943 until 1992: SFRY

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tisъ, of disputed origin.
